mainEntity.name: What number systems does Java support?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java supports four number systems natively: Decimal (base 10) — the default, written as plain integers like 255; Binary (base 2) — written with the 0b or 0B prefix, e.g. 0b11111111; Octal (base 8) — written with a leading 0, e.g. 0377; Hexadecimal (base 16) — written with 0x or 0X prefix, e.g. 0xFF. All four represent the same integer value (255) and are stored identically in memory as 32-bit int. Java also supports binary literals with underscores for readability: 0b1111_1111.

mainEntity.name: How do you convert decimal to binary in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java provides multiple ways: (1) Integer.toBinaryString(n) — returns binary string without sign bit, e.g. Integer.toBinaryString(25) returns '11001'. (2) Integer.toString(n, 2) — converts to binary string with radix 2. (3) Manual loop: while (n > 0) { sb.append(n % 2); n /= 2; } then reverse the StringBuilder. (4) String.format('%s', Integer.toBinaryString(n)). For padding to 8 bits: String.format('%8s', Integer.toBinaryString(n)).replace(' ', '0').

mainEntity.name: What is two's complement in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Two's complement is Java's standard method for representing negative integers in binary. To find the two's complement of a negative number: (1) Write the binary of the absolute value; (2) Flip all bits (one's complement); (3) Add 1 to the result. For example, -5 in 8-bit: 5 = 00000101, flip = 11111010, add 1 = 11111011. Java's int is 32-bit two's complement, ranging from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. Integer.toBinaryString(-1) returns 32 ones because -1 in two's complement is all 1s.

mainEntity.name: How do you convert a binary string to decimal in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use Integer.parseInt(binaryString, 2). For example: Integer.parseInt('11001', 2) returns 25. The second argument is the radix (base). Similarly: Integer.parseInt('377', 8) converts octal string '377' to decimal 255. Integer.parseInt('FF', 16) converts hex string 'FF' to decimal 255. For larger values, use Long.parseLong(string, radix) to handle numbers beyond Integer.MAX_VALUE.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between >> and >>> in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: >>' is the signed right shift operator — it shifts bits right and fills the leftmost bits with the sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negative). So -8 >> 1 gives -4. '>>>' is the unsigned right shift operator — it always fills the leftmost bits with 0 regardless of the sign bit. So -8 >>> 1 gives a large positive number (2147483644 for 32-bit int). Use >> for arithmetic division by powers of 2; use >>> when you need logical (unsigned) bit shifting, especially when working with bit masks and flags.

articleHeader.title: Java Number System
articleHeader.subtitle: A complete guide to the Java Number System — binary, octal, decimal, hexadecimal representations, base conversion methods, number literals, two's complement for negative numbers, bitwise and shift operators, and real-world applications with practical examples.

blocks.text: A number system is a mathematical framework for representing quantities using a fixed set of digits and a base (also called radix). The base determines how many unique digits are available and how positional value is assigned to each digit. Every position in a number represents a power of the base — just like how the '3' in '300' means 3 × 10² in decimal.

Computers — including the JVM that runs Java programs — operate entirely on binary (base 2): every piece of data, every instruction, every character in memory is ultimately represented as a sequence of bits (0s and 1s). As a Java developer, understanding number systems means understanding how the data you write in code (int x = 255) is actually stored and manipulated at the hardware level — and how to work with that binary representation directly when needed.

Java natively supports four number systems in source code: decimal (base 10, everyday use), binary (base 2, bit-level operations), octal (base 8, legacy Unix permissions), and hexadecimal (base 16, memory addresses, colour codes, cryptographic hashes). All four compile to identical machine instructions — they are simply different ways of writing the same integer value in source code.

blocks.text: Understanding number systems is not academic theory — it has direct, daily practical applications in professional Java development:

items.text: — RGB colours in web and Android development are written in hexadecimal: #FF5733 means Red=0xFF (255), Green=0x57 (87), Blue=0x33 (51). Java AWT and Android's Color class accept hex values like 0xFF5733.

— SHA-256, MD5, and other hash outputs are hex strings: e.g. 'a9993e36476...' Each hex character represents 4 bits (a nibble), making hex the most compact human-readable representation of byte arrays.

— Linux file permissions (chmod 755 = rwxr-xr-x) are octal. Java's NIO FilePermissions, Android's Manifest permissions, and network flag fields use bit manipulation where understanding binary layout is essential.
— JVM memory addresses, object references in debugging output (e.g. Object@1b6d3586), and native memory operations via JNI or Java's Unsafe class all use hexadecimal.
— Fast power-of-2 operations, bitmask flags, low-level protocol parsing (TCP headers, USB HID reports), and embedded systems interfaces all require direct binary manipulation.
— Reading binary file formats (PNG, ZIP, class files), network packets, or hardware sensor data requires understanding how bytes (8 bits each) map to integer values across different bases.

Key insight: One hexadecimal digit represents exactly 4 binary bits (a nibble). One octal digit represents exactly 3 binary bits. This is why hex is so popular for representing bytes — one byte (8 bits) is always exactly two hex digits (e.g., 0xFF = 1111 1111 = 255).

Java allows integer literals to be written in all four bases directly in source code. Java 7 also added underscore separators inside numeric literals to improve readability — the underscores are ignored by the compiler.

blocks.text: Important rules for underscores in literals: Underscores cannot appear at the start or end of a literal (_255 and 255_ are invalid). They cannot appear adjacent to the decimal point in floating-point literals (3._14 is invalid). They cannot appear before the L, f, or d suffix. Other than these restrictions, underscores can appear anywhere — including in hex, binary, and octal literals.

sections.title: Best Practices for Java Number Systems

blocks.text: Professional Java developers follow these best practices to write clear, correct, and portable code when working with number systems and bit manipulation:

items.strong: ✅ 1. Use Binary Literals for Bit Flags and Masks
items.text: — When defining bit masks or flags, write them in binary (0b1000_0000) not decimal (128) or hex (0x80). Binary literals make the bit structure immediately visible without mental translation.

items.strong: ✅ 2. Use Hex for Byte Values and Colour Codes
items.text: — One byte (8 bits) = two hex digits. Use 0xFF not 255 when working with byte arrays, colour components, or protocol fields. Hex communicates byte boundaries clearly.

items.strong: ✅ 3. Use Underscore Separators for Large Literals
items.text: — Write 1_000_000 not 1000000, 0xFF_FF not 0xFFFF, and 0b1010_0101 not 0b10100101. Underscores dramatically improve readability for constants, bitmasks, and large numbers.

items.strong: ✅ 4. Use >>> Instead of >> for Unsigned Operations
items.text: — When shifting for bit extraction or hash computation (not arithmetic division), use >>> to avoid accidental sign extension. >>> always fills with 0; >> extends the sign bit. Java's HashMap uses >>> 16 in its hash spreading — not >>.

— Java's built-in Integer.toBinaryString(), Integer.toHexString(), and Integer.parseInt(s, radix) are faster, tested, and handles edge cases (0, negative values) correctly. Use manual algorithms only in interviews or when custom formatting is needed.

items.strong: ✅ 6. Be Aware of Integer Overflow in Bit Operations
items.text: — Left-shifting a value past the sign bit causes overflow. int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE; max << 1; wraps around. For values that might overflow, use long literals and Long arithmetic, or check bounds before shifting.

items.strong: ✅ 7. Use EnumSet Instead of int Bitmasks for Flags in Production
items.text: — While int bitmasks are fast and concise, EnumSet<MyFlags> provides type safety, readable names, and efficient bit operations under the hood. Prefer EnumSet for domain flag management in production Java code.

items.strong: ❌ 8. Never Use Octal Literals for Non-Permission Values
items.text: — A leading zero on an integer literal makes it octal: int x = 010 means 8, not 10! This is a notorious Java gotcha. Only use octal literals intentionally for file permission constants. Never write leading-zero decimal numbers.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Working with Number Systems in Java

blocks.text: Understanding and using multiple number systems in Java brings concrete benefits — but also requires careful handling to avoid subtle bugs.

pros.title: Native Multi-Base Literal Support
pros.text: Java directly supports binary (0b), octal (0), and hexadecimal (0x) literals in source code. No conversion needed — write 0xFF and Java stores it identically to 255 in memory. This makes hardware, colour, and flag constants self-documenting.

pros.title: Bitwise Operations Enable High Performance
pros.text: Bit manipulation (AND, OR, XOR, shifts) is the fastest category of CPU instruction — no division, no branching. Checking even/odd with (n & 1), power-of-2 checks with (n & (n-1)) == 0, and bit flag operations are orders of magnitude faster than arithmetic equivalents.

pros.title: Rich Integer Utility API
pros.text: Integer.toBinaryString(), toHexString(), parseInt(s, radix), bitCount(), numberOfLeadingZeros() and 10+ other methods provide ready-made, tested tools for all common number-system operations without manual implementation.

pros.title: Direct Hardware and Protocol Compatibility
pros.text: Network protocols, file formats, and hardware interfaces communicate in bytes and bit fields. Binary and hex literacy lets you read and write protocol specifications directly and parse binary data formats without translation layers.

pros.title: Underscore Literals Improve Code Readability
pros.text: Java 7+ underscore separators (1_000_000, 0xFF_FF_FF, 0b1010_0101) make large constants, colour codes, and bitmasks instantly readable without magic number comments.

cons.title: Octal Literal Gotcha — Leading Zero
cons.text: A leading zero silently makes any integer literal octal: int x = 010; means x = 8, not 10. This is a notorious Java bug source. Never write decimal numbers with leading zeros — use explicit octal only for permission constants where the context is unambiguous.

cons.title: Signed vs Unsigned Confusion
cons.text: Java has no unsigned int type (unlike C/C++). All int operations are signed two's complement. Shifting -1 >> 1 gives -1 (sign extension), not a large positive. Using >>> instead of >> for unsigned logic is non-obvious to beginners and a common bug source.

cons.title: Integer Overflow Is Silent
cons.text: Java does not throw an exception on integer overflow — it silently wraps around. Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 gives Integer.MIN_VALUE with no warning. Left-shifting past the sign bit corrupts values silently. Overflow-safe arithmetic requires explicit checks or Math.addExact() / Math.multiplyExact().

cons.title: Binary Manipulation Code Is Hard to Read
cons.text: Complex bitmask expressions like (perms & ~(READ | WRITE)) | EXECUTE require careful documentation. Without clear constant names and comments, bitwise code becomes unmaintainable. Always use named constants (static final int READ = 0b0001) instead of raw literals.

blocks.text: These are the most frequently asked interview questions on the Java Number System and related bit manipulation for Java developer and competitive programming interviews.

items.q: Q1. What number systems does Java support, and how are they written in source code?
items.a: Java supports four number systems: Decimal (base 10) — no prefix, e.g. 255. Binary (base 2) — prefix 0b or 0B, e.g. 0b11111111. Octal (base 8) — leading zero prefix, e.g. 0377. Hexadecimal (base 16) — prefix 0x or 0X, e.g. 0xFF. All four represent the same integer in memory and are interchangeable in expressions. Java 7+ also allows underscore separators inside literals for readability: 0b1111_1111, 0xFF_FF, 1_000_000.

items.q: Q2. How do you convert a decimal number to binary in Java — in 3 different ways?
items.a: (1) Integer.toBinaryString(n) — built-in, returns unsigned binary string. (2) Integer.toString(n, 2) — radix-based, returns signed binary string for negatives. (3) Manual loop — repeatedly divide by 2, collect remainders, reverse: StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); while (n > 0) { sb.append(n % 2); n /= 2; } sb.reverse(). For padding to 8 bits: String.format('%8s', Integer.toBinaryString(n)).replace(' ', '0').

items.q: Q3. What is two's complement and why does Java use it?
items.a: Two's complement is the standard binary representation for negative integers. To find -n: flip all bits of n then add 1. Java uses it for all integer types (byte, short, int, long). Benefits: (1) Only one representation of zero (unlike sign-magnitude). (2) Addition and subtraction hardware works identically for positive and negative numbers — no special case logic. (3) Overflow wraps naturally. Java's int range is -2^31 to 2^31-1 because the MSB is the sign bit.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between >> and >>> in Java?
items.a: >> is the signed right shift. It shifts bits right and fills the vacated MSBs with the sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negative). So -8 >> 1 = -4 (arithmetic division by 2, sign preserved). >>> is the unsigned right shift. It always fills vacated MSBs with 0 regardless of sign. So -8 >>> 1 gives 2147483644 (a large positive number). Use >> for arithmetic operations on signed integers; use >>> for bit manipulation, hash spreading, and unsigned byte operations.

items.q: Q5. What is the output of: System.out.println(010 + 010); — and why?
items.a: 16. In Java, an integer literal with a leading zero is octal (base 8). 010 in octal = 8 in decimal. So 010 + 010 = 8 + 8 = 16. This is a classic Java gotcha interview trap. Never write decimal numbers with leading zeros. If you intend octal, use it explicitly with a clear comment: int unixPerms = 0755; // Unix rwxr-xr-x

items.q: Q6. How do you check if a number is a power of 2 using bitwise operations?
items.a: Use (n > 0) && ((n & (n - 1)) == 0). Explanation: a power of 2 in binary has exactly one bit set (e.g., 8 = 1000). n - 1 flips all bits below that bit (8-1 = 7 = 0111). n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit — for powers of 2, the result is always 0. The n > 0 guard handles the edge case n = 0 (which satisfies (n & (n-1)) == 0 but is not a power of 2).

items.q: Q7. What does Integer.toBinaryString(-1) return, and why?
items.a: It returns '11111111111111111111111111111111' — 32 ones. In Java's 32-bit two's complement representation, -1 is all 1-bits. This is because -1 = ~0 (bitwise NOT of 0). toBinaryString() shows the actual binary representation without a sign or padding. This is why Integer.bitCount(-1) returns 32 — all 32 bits are 1.

items.q: Q8. Write the bit manipulation expression to: (a) set bit k, (b) clear bit k, (c) toggle bit k, (d) check if bit k is set.
items.a: (a) Set bit k: n | (1 << k) — ORing with a mask that has only bit k set. (b) Clear bit k: n & ~(1 << k) — ANDing with a mask that has all bits set except k. (c) Toggle bit k: n ^ (1 << k) — XORing with a mask flips bit k. (d) Check if bit k is set: (n & (1 << k)) != 0 — AND with mask; non-zero means set. These four operations form the foundation of all bit flag management and are tested in virtually every systems programming interview.

items.q: Q9. What is Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 in Java, and why?
items.a: Integer.MIN_VALUE (-2147483648). This is integer overflow — a two's complement wrap-around. Integer.MAX_VALUE = 0111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 in binary. Adding 1 sets all mantissa bits to 0 and the sign bit to 1: 1000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 = Integer.MIN_VALUE. Java does not throw an exception — overflow is silent. Use Math.addExact(a, b) to get ArithmeticException on overflow, or switch to long for larger values.

items.q: Q10. How do you count the number of set bits (1-bits) in an integer efficiently?
items.a: Method 1: Integer.bitCount(n) — Java's built-in O(1) population count using hardware intrinsic. Method 2: Brian Kernighan's algorithm — while (n != 0) { n &= (n - 1); count++; } — each iteration clears the lowest set bit; runs in O(k) where k is number of set bits. Method 3: naive loop — check each bit: for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) if ((n & (1 << i)) != 0) count++; — O(32). Always use Integer.bitCount() in production; know Kernighan's for interviews.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of Java Number Systems with these practice questions. Attempt each before revealing the answer.

items.q: 1. What are the decimal values of: (a) 0b1010 (b) 0777 (c) 0x1F (d) 0b1111_0000?

2. What is the output?
int x = 0b1010;  // 10
int y = 0b1100;  // 12
System.out.println(x & y);  // AND
System.out.println(x | y);  // OR
System.out.println(x ^ y);  // XOR
items.a: 8, 14, 6. AND: 1010 & 1100 = 1000 = 8. OR: 1010 | 1100 = 1110 = 14. XOR: 1010 ^ 1100 = 0110 = 6. Bit-by-bit: AND gives 1 only if both bits are 1; OR gives 1 if either is 1; XOR gives 1 if exactly one bit is 1.

items.q: 3. Why does int x = 09; cause a compile error but int y = 07; does not?
items.a: A leading zero makes the literal octal (base 8). Octal digits are only 0–7. The digit '9' does not exist in base 8, so 09 is an invalid octal literal and causes a compile error. 07 is a valid octal literal = 7 in decimal. This is why you should never write decimal integers with a leading zero unless you intentionally mean octal.

items.q: 4. Write a Java expression to extract the lower byte (bits 0–7) and upper byte (bits 8–15) of an int using bitwise operators.
items.a: Lower byte: int lower = n & 0xFF; — masks all bits above bit 7. Upper byte: int upper = (n >> 8) & 0xFF; — right shift by 8 to move bits 8–15 to positions 0–7, then mask. Example: n = 0x1A2B → lower = 0x2B = 43; upper = 0x1A = 26. This pattern is fundamental in network protocol parsing and binary file I/O.

items.q: 5. What does n & (n-1) compute? What is it useful for?
items.a: n & (n-1) clears (turns off) the lowest set bit (rightmost 1-bit) of n. Example: n = 12 = 1100, n-1 = 11 = 1011, n & (n-1) = 1000 = 8. Uses: (1) Check if n is a power of 2: (n > 0) && (n & (n-1)) == 0. (2) Count set bits (Kernighan's algorithm): repeat n &= (n-1) until n == 0, counting iterations. (3) Check if n has exactly one set bit. This is one of the most tested bitwise tricks in interviews.

items.q: 6. What is the output of Integer.toBinaryString(-5) and why does it have 32 characters?
items.a: 11111111111111111111111111111011. Java's int is 32-bit two's complement. -5 = ~5 + 1 = flip(00000101) + 1 = 11111010 + 1 = 11111011 (8-bit). In 32-bit: 11111111111111111111111111111011. toBinaryString() shows the actual 32-bit representation for negatives (no leading zeros are stripped for negative numbers since all 32 bits are meaningful in two's complement).

items.q: 7. A 32-bit int stores an RGBA colour as: bits 31-24 = Alpha, bits 23-16 = Red, bits 15-8 = Green, bits 7-0 = Blue. Write expressions to extract each component.
items.a:
int alpha = (colour >>> 24) & 0xFF;  // unsigned shift — Alpha in bits 31-24
int red   = (colour >> 16) & 0xFF;   // bits 23-16
int green = (colour >> 8)  & 0xFF;   // bits 15-8
int blue  =  colour        & 0xFF;   // bits 7-0
Note: >>> is used for Alpha to handle the case where bit 31 is set (the sign bit) — >> would sign-extend and give wrong results for alpha > 127.

items.q: 8. Without using any division operator (/) or modulo (%), determine if an integer n is even or odd using bitwise operations. Explain why it works.
items.a: boolean isEven = (n & 1) == 0; The binary representation of any integer ends in 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd numbers (since 2^0 = 1 is the only odd power of 2). ANDing with 1 (binary: ...0001) isolates the least significant bit. If LSB = 0, the number is even; if LSB = 1, the number is odd. This is faster than n % 2 == 0 because AND is a single CPU instruction with no division involved.

blocks.text: The number system is the bedrock of computer science — and Java's first-class support for binary, octal, decimal, and hexadecimal literals, combined with its rich Integer utility methods and bitwise operator set, gives you every tool needed to work directly at the bit level when required.

Mastering number systems in Java means knowing when to use binary literals for bit flags, hexadecimal for byte values and colour codes, and underscore separators for readable constants. It means understanding two's complement to predict overflow behaviour, using >>> correctly for unsigned shifts, and leveraging bit tricks like n & (n-1) for high-performance operations in competitive programming and systems code.

Remember: Binary (0b) for flags, Hex (0x) for bytes, underscore separators for readability, >>> for unsigned shifts, and always name your bit constants. These five habits will keep your number system code correct, readable, and professional. ☕

items.q: What is two's complement in Java?
items.a: Two's complement is Java's standard method for representing negative integers in binary. To find the two's complement: write the binary of the absolute value, flip all bits (one's complement), then add 1. Java's int is 32-bit two's complement, ranging from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. Integer.toBinaryString(-1) returns 32 ones because -1 in two's complement is all 1s.

items.q: How do you convert a binary string to decimal in Java?
items.a: Use Integer.parseInt(binaryString, 2). For example: Integer.parseInt('11001', 2) returns 25. Similarly: Integer.parseInt('377', 8) converts octal '377' to 255. Integer.parseInt('FF', 16) converts hex 'FF' to 255. For larger values, use Long.parseLong(string, radix).

items.q: What is the difference between >> and >>> in Java?
items.a: '>>' is the signed right shift — fills leftmost bits with the sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negative). So -8 >> 1 gives -4. '>>>' is the unsigned right shift — always fills leftmost bits with 0 regardless of sign. Use >> for arithmetic division by powers of 2; use >>> when you need logical bit shifting, especially for bit masks and hash functions.
